Showing Distributions

Boxplots, violins & ridgelines · Day 01

Choosing a Distribution Plot

Showing distributions · what to plot when

Six lenses on a single variable

Histogram

Counts in bins. Raw shape; sensitive to bin width.

Density (KDE)

Smoothed shape. Best for overlaying a few groups.

Boxplot

Five-number summary. Compact across many groups.

Violin

Density mirrored. Shape + summary in one footprint.

Strip / sina

Every point shown. Honest when n is small.

Ridgeline

Distributions stacked across groups or time.

Rule of thumb Small n → strip · few groups → density or histogram · many groups → boxplot or ridgeline · need shape and summary → violin.

When & Why a Boxplot

Distributions · when to use

A boxplot summarises spread, pick the chart that fits your question

Use a boxplot to compare the distribution of a continuous value across a few groups — its centre, spread, and outliers — without plotting every point.

Spread is not precision. SD describes how the data scatter around the mean; SE describes how precise your estimate of the mean is. A boxplot answers the first question; error bars on a mean answer the second.

r = np.random.default_rng(1)
groups = ["WT", "Mut A", "Mut B"]
data = [r.normal(50, 6, 70),                # WT
        r.normal(62, 10, 70),               # Mut A — bigger spread
        r.normal(58, 4, 70)]                # Mut B — tighter

SD vs SE: spread of the data vs precision of the estimate. Same numbers, different question, different chart. (Wilke 2019, Ch. 9)

Building a Boxplot · Step 1: the canvas

Distributions · boxplot build

Set up the figure, labels, and scale before any data

Start with an empty, labelled canvas: axes, group positions, y-scale. Decide the frame first, fill it after.

groups = ["WT", "Mut A", "Mut B"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.7))
ax.set_ylabel("Expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xticks([1, 2, 3])
ax.set_xticklabels(groups)
ax.set_xlim(0.5, 3.5)
ax.set_ylim(30, 85)

Building a Boxplot · Step 2: the raw points

Distributions · boxplot build

Look at the data first, with a little horizontal jitter

Plot every observation, jittering x-position so points don’t stack on one line. This shows the sample size and shape that a summary will later hide.

# data: list of three np.ndarrays, one per group
rj = np.random.default_rng(2)
for i, d in enumerate(data, start=1):
    x = rj.normal(i, 0.06, len(d))           # gentle jitter
    ax.scatter(x, d,
               color=GREEN, s=18,
               alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")

Building a Boxplot · Step 3: add the box

Distributions · boxplot build

Overlay the five-number summary on top of the points

The box draws Q1 → Q3, the median line, and whiskers to the most extreme points within 1.5 × IQR. Matplotlib computes all of it for you.

bp = ax.boxplot(
    data,
    positions=[1, 2, 3],
    widths=0.5,
    patch_artist=True,        # so we can colour it
)

Building a Boxplot · Step 4: style on-palette

Distributions · boxplot build

Economist green box, ink median, fade the points behind

Style every element: a soft teal fill, a green edge, a bold ink median, green whiskers. Drop the alpha on the points so the box reads on top.

bp = ax.boxplot(data, positions=[1,2,3], widths=0.5, patch_artist=True)
for p in bp["boxes"]:
    p.set_facecolor(ECON["hongkong"][3])
    p.set_edgecolor(GREEN); p.set_alpha(0.75)
for m in bp["medians"]:
    m.set_color(INK); m.set_linewidth(2)
for w in bp["whiskers"] + bp["caps"]:
    w.set_color(GREEN)

Building a Boxplot · Step 5: the message

Distributions · boxplot build

Hide duplicate outliers, title the finding

The points already show every value, so turn off the default flier markers. Finish with a title that says what the reader should take away.

bp = ax.boxplot(data, showfliers=False, ...)
ax.set_title("MUT A SHOWS THE WIDEST SPREAD")

That’s the whole recipe: canvas → points → box → style → message.

When & Why a Violin

Distributions · when to use

Reach for a violin when the shape matters, not just the summary

A boxplot hides shape — two very different distributions can share the same five-number summary. A violin draws a mirrored density, so a second hump or a long skew is visible at a glance.

Use it when the distribution might be bimodal or strongly skewed. Use a plain boxplot when a clean five-number summary is all you need.

The boxplot shows the summary. The violin shows the shape. Bimodality is the story the box can’t tell. (Wilke 2019, Ch. 7)

Building a Violin · Step 1: the canvas

Distributions · violin build

Same canvas as the boxplot, three groups, one deliberately bimodal

The recipe starts identically: an empty, labelled frame. One group is deliberately bimodal so the violin has something a box would hide.

r = np.random.default_rng(3)
groups = ["WT", "Mut A", "Mut B"]
data = [np.concatenate([r.normal(45, 5, 45),
                        r.normal(62, 5, 35)]),  # WT is bimodal
        r.normal(62, 10, 80),
        r.normal(58,  4, 80)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.7))

Building a Violin · Step 2: the raw points

Distributions · violin build

Jittered points already hint at the bimodality

The WT group sits in two clouds, not one. The violin will make that explicit.

rj = np.random.default_rng(4)
for i, d in enumerate(data, start=1):
    ax.scatter(rj.normal(i, 0.06, len(d)), d,
               color=GREEN, s=16, alpha=0.5,
               edgecolors="none")

Building a Violin · Step 3: add the density

Distributions · violin build

violinplot draws a kernel density and mirrors it about each axis

The body width at any height is the point density there. The WT violin now shows two bulges, the bimodality a box would flatten away.

vp = ax.violinplot(
    data,
    positions=[1, 2, 3],
    showextrema=False,
)

Building a Violin · Step 4: style on-palette

Distributions · violin build

Teal body, green edge, fade the points behind

Loop over the violin bodies and colour them on-brand, then drop the points’ alpha so the density reads on top.

vp = ax.violinplot(data, positions=[1,2,3], showextrema=False)
for b in vp["bodies"]:
    b.set_facecolor(ECON["hongkong"][3])
    b.set_edgecolor(GREEN)
    b.set_alpha(0.75)
    b.set_linewidth(1.4)

Building a Violin · Step 5: the message

Distributions · violin build

Slim inner boxplot for the summary, title the finding

A thin boxplot inside each violin gives the five-number summary and the shape together. Finish with the takeaway in the title.

for i, d in enumerate(data, start=1):
    bx = ax.boxplot(d, positions=[i],
                    widths=0.1, patch_artist=True,
                    showfliers=False)
    bx["boxes"][0].set_facecolor(INK)
    bx["medians"][0].set_color(CREAM)
ax.set_title("WT IS BIMODAL")

Same recipe as the box: canvas → points → density → style → message.

Box vs violin: the box gives the summary, the violin reveals the shape. Show the violin when bimodality or skew is the story.

Ridgeline · The Data

Distributions · ridgeline

2,000 single cells, ordered along a trajectory

load_pseudotime() is single-cell data in tidy long form: one row per cell. Each cell has a pseudotime stage (1 = earliest, 8 = latest along the differentiation path) and the marker gene’s expression. With 250 cells per stage, every stage is a proper distribution, not a single number.

from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()        # cell, stage, expression
print(pt.shape)               # 2000 cells × 3 columns
pt.head(4)
(2000, 3)
cell stage expression
0 S1_000 1 1.607084
1 S1_001 1 1.846248
2 S1_002 1 1.994292
3 S1_003 1 1.623597

Ridgeline · See the Cells First

Distributions · ridgeline

Before any smoothing: one dot per cell

Plot every cell as a dot, expression on the x-axis, stage on the y-axis with a little jitter. Early stages sit in a low cloud (gene OFF); late stages sit in a high cloud (gene ON); the middle stages show both clouds at once, that’s the bimodal hand-off. The ridgeline next just replaces each row of dots with a smooth density.

from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()                                     # 2000 cells: cell, stage, expression
stages = sorted(pt.stage.unique())                         # ordered pseudotime stages 1..8
n = len(stages)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)                             # reproducible jitter

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.0))
for i, s in enumerate(stages):                             # one row of dots per stage
    vals = pt.loc[pt.stage == s, "expression"].values      # this stage's cells
    y = i + rng.uniform(-0.32, 0.32, len(vals))            # jitter so dots don't pile on one line
    ax.scatter(vals, y, s=6, color=econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1)),  # x = expression, one dot per cell
               alpha=.35, linewidths=0)                    # low alpha shows where cells pile up
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"stage {s}" for s in stages], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("NEUROD1 expression"); ax.set_ylabel("pseudotime →")
ax.set_xlim(0, 12)
for sp in ["top", "right", "left"]:                        # bare frame, same look as the ridgeline
    ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("each dot is one cell", color=MUTED, fontsize=11, loc="left")
plt.show()

Ridgelines

Many distributions, one panel · Day 01

When a Ridgeline

Distributions · theory

Watch a distribution change across an ordered factor

A ridgeline stacks one density per group, slightly overlapping, so you compare many distributions in a compact panel. It earns its place when the groups have a meaningful order and the distribution shifts across it: expression along pseudotime, a signal across tissues, a metric over time. The shape is the story, a mode appearing, a peak sliding right.

Two requirements keep it honest: enough points per group for a smooth density (a KDE on twenty values is noise), and a colour ramp keyed to the group order so the eye follows the progression instead of decoding a rainbow. Here: a neural marker switching on as cells differentiate.

Ridgeline · The Data

Distributions · ridgeline

A marker gene across single cells, ordered by pseudotime

load_pseudotime() is tidy long: one row per cell, its pseudotime stage (1 = earliest), and the marker’s expression. Each stage is a distribution we’ll turn into one ridge.

from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()   # cell, stage, expression
pt.head(4)
cell stage expression
0 S1_000 1 1.607084
1 S1_001 1 1.846248
2 S1_002 1 1.994292
3 S1_003 1 1.623597

Ridgeline · Step 1 — A Density Per Stage

Distributions · build

1 · KDE each group

Smooth each stage’s expression into a density with gaussian_kde, on a shared x-grid, and normalise to the same height so shapes are comparable. Overlaid, you can already see a second hump appear, but they collide.

from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde                       # kernel density estimator
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()                                     # cell, stage, expression
stages = sorted(pt.stage.unique())                         # ordered pseudotime stages 1..8
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)                               # shared grid for every density

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 4.7))                 # one panel
for s in stages:                                           # one KDE per stage
    vals = pt.loc[pt.stage == s, "expression"].values      # this stage's cells
    k = gaussian_kde(vals)(xs)                              # smooth density over xs
    ax.plot(xs, k / k.max(), color=GREEN, lw=1.2, alpha=.6)  # normalise height; all overlaid
ax.set_xlabel("NEUROD1 expression"); ax.set_ylabel("density (normalised)")
plt.show()

Ridgeline · Step 2 — Stack the Ridges

Distributions · build

2 · Offset and fill

Give each density its own baseline y = i and fill_between it, scaled by overlap (>1 so neighbours touch). Colour by stage along econ_spectrum, and the zorder puts lower ridges in front. Now they read as a stack.

from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()                                     # cell, stage, expression
stages = sorted(pt.stage.unique())                         # ordered stages
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)                               # shared grid
n = len(stages); overlap = 1.8                             # ridge height (>1 → ridges overlap)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.2))
for i, s in enumerate(stages):                             # stage 1 at the bottom, 8 at the top
    vals = pt.loc[pt.stage == s, "expression"].values      # this stage's cells
    k = gaussian_kde(vals)(xs); k = k / k.max() * overlap  # normalise, then scale to ridge height
    col = econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1))                       # colour keyed to pseudotime order
    ax.fill_between(xs, i + k, i, color=col, alpha=.8,     # ridge sits on baseline y = i
                    lw=1, edgecolor=CREAM, zorder=n - i)    # lower ridges drawn in front
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"stage {s}" for s in stages], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("NEUROD1 expression"); ax.set_ylabel("pseudotime →")
ax.set_xlim(0, 12)
plt.show()

Ridgeline · Step 3 — The Message

Distributions · build

3 · Clean edge, no frame, name the finding

Trace each ridge’s top in cream so overlaps stay crisp, drop the frame (ridgelines read better bare), and title with the result. The OFF→bimodal→ON march is the whole point.

from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
from genomics_course.data import load_pseudotime

pt = load_pseudotime()                                     # cell, stage, expression
stages = sorted(pt.stage.unique())                         # ordered stages
xs = np.linspace(0, 12, 300)                               # shared grid
n = len(stages); overlap = 1.8                             # ridge height

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.2))
for i, s in enumerate(stages):                             # bottom → top
    vals = pt.loc[pt.stage == s, "expression"].values      # this stage's cells
    k = gaussian_kde(vals)(xs); k = k / k.max() * overlap  # normalised, scaled density
    col = econ_spectrum(i / (n - 1))                       # spectrum keyed to order
    ax.fill_between(xs, i + k, i, color=col, alpha=.8, lw=1, edgecolor=CREAM, zorder=n - i)
    ax.plot(xs, i + k, color=CREAM, lw=.8, zorder=n - i)   # crisp cream top edge per ridge
ax.set_yticks(range(n)); ax.set_yticklabels([f"stage {s}" for s in stages], fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("NEUROD1 expression"); ax.set_ylabel("pseudotime →")
ax.set_xlim(0, 12); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, n + overlap)         # headroom for the top ridge
for sp in ["top", "right", "left"]:                        # ridgelines read better frameless
    ax.spines[sp].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("NEUROD1 SWITCHES ON ALONG THE TRAJECTORY",   # title states the finding
             color=GREEN, fontweight="bold", loc="left")
plt.show()

The bottom line A ridgeline is many densities stacked along an ordered factor: KDE each group → offset and fill → ramp keyed to order. Watch the marker switch on, a single OFF hump, a bimodal transition where some cells flip, then a single ON hump. The shift is the result.

Exercise · Library QC

Distributions · exercise

Are the libraries comparable?

Real scenario Before differential expression, you check that every sample’s expression distribution looks alike, a ridge sitting clearly left or right of the rest flags a library that needs normalising. Melt load_expression() to long and build one ridge per sample, coloured by condition.

from scipy.stats import gaussian_kde
from genomics_course.data import load_expression

expr = load_expression()                                   # genes × samples
long = expr.melt(var_name="sample", value_name="expr")     # one row per gene-sample

# 1. xs over the expression range; samples = expr.columns
# 2. for each sample i: k = gaussian_kde(values); fill_between(xs, i + k/k.max(), i)
# 3. colour by condition: BLUE if name starts with "C", AMBER if "D"
# 4. read it: does any sample's ridge sit offset from the rest? → normalise before DE

Building a Plot

A scatter, step by step · Day 01

Building a Plot · The Data

The Python viz stack · what we’re plotting

How the data loads

load_coexpression() returns one row per sample: two gene expression values plus the tissue it came from. Three tissues, Leaf / Root / Seed.

from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()        # sample, tissue, gene_x, gene_y
co.head(3)
sample tissue gene_x gene_y
0 Leaf_7110 Leaf 3.715459 4.780508
1 Leaf_9330 Leaf 5.334575 6.522094
2 Leaf_8607 Leaf 8.461562 12.642475

Building a Plot · Step 1 — The Canvas

The Python viz stack · building a figure

1 · Canvas

We’ll build a scatter: gene Y against gene X, one dot per sample. Start with a figure and an axes, then frame the axes before drawing anything.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))   # one figure, one axes
ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")     # frame the axes before drawing
ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Building a Plot · Step 2 — Load & Plot Data

The Python viz stack · building a figure

2 · Data

Load the samples and drop them onto the canvas with ax.scatter(). One dot per sample, default colour for now.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()                     # sample, tissue, gene_x, gene_y

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
ax.scatter(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, color=GREY, s=50, alpha=.8)   # one dot per sample
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Building a Plot · Step 3 — Colour by Tissue

The Python viz stack · building a figure

3 · Colour

Loop over the tissues, one pass each, one palette colour each. Colour now carries real signal, the tissues separate.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}   # one colour per tissue
for tissue, c in pal.items():
    g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
    ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")     # name the tissues
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Building a Plot · Step 4 — Polish & Labels

The Python viz stack · building a figure

4 · Polish

A single linear fit across all samples summarises the trend. Compute slope and intercept, draw it in red, and let the title state what we found.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
for tissue, c in pal.items():
    g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
    ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)             # single linear fit
xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)   # draw it in red
ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")  # state the finding
ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Building a Plot · Step 5 — Style Once, Reuse Everywhere

The Python viz stack · building a figure

5 · House style

Bundle your spine and grid choices into one block and apply it. The per-axes spine code disappears, every plot inherits the same look.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {                                    # the house style, defined ONCE
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):                  # apply it: no per-axes spine code
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()

Building a Plot · Step 7 — Drop the Vertical Grid

The Python viz stack · building a figure

7 · Grid

Keep the horizontal gridlines as value guides, drop the verticals. Fewer competing lines, the eye reads the y values cleanly.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.35, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.xaxis.grid(False)                     # keep horizontal guides, drop verticals
    ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")

Building a Plot · Step 8 — Point At It

The Python viz stack · building a figure

8 · Arrow

Find the sample furthest above the fit, then aim a curved annotate arrow at it. The rad bends the arrow so it comes in from the side instead of crossing the dot.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.35, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.xaxis.grid(False)
    co["resid"] = co.gene_y - (m * co.gene_x + b)   # distance from the fit
    hot = co.loc[co.resid.idxmax()]                 # furthest sample above it
    ax.annotate(f"{hot.tissue} outlier", xy=(hot.gene_x, hot.gene_y),
                xytext=(hot.gene_x - 3.2, hot.gene_y + 2.0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=INK, lw=1.6,
                                connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.3"))   # curved callout
    ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()

Building a Plot · Step 9 — Highlight the Sample

The Python viz stack · building a figure

9 · Edge

Re-draw that one sample with a thick white edge. The wall lifts it off the crowd the arrow is pointing at.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.35, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.xaxis.grid(False)
    co["resid"] = co.gene_y - (m * co.gene_x + b)
    hot = co.loc[co.resid.idxmax()]
    ax.annotate(f"{hot.tissue} outlier", xy=(hot.gene_x, hot.gene_y),
                xytext=(hot.gene_x - 3.2, hot.gene_y + 2.0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=INK, lw=1.6,
                                connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.3"))
    ax.scatter(hot.gene_x, hot.gene_y, s=120, color=pal[hot.tissue],   # re-draw it
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=2.2, zorder=5)             # white wall pops it
    ax.set_title("Gene Y tracks gene X", color="#333333")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()

Building a Plot · Step 10 — Title, Subtitle, Caption

The Python viz stack · building a figure

10 · Header

Layer the text the way an editorial figure does: a bold title, an italic subtitle, and a small caption crediting the source.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()

house = {
    "axes.spines.top":   False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "axes.grid":         True,
    "grid.linestyle":    "--",
    "grid.color":        LINE,
}
with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.8))
    ax.set_xlabel("gene X expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_ylabel("gene Y expression (TPM)")
    ax.set_xlim(1, 11); ax.set_ylim(-1, 17)
    pal = {"Leaf": GREEN, "Root": BLUE, "Seed": AMBER}
    for tissue, c in pal.items():
        g = co[co.tissue == tissue]
        ax.scatter(g.gene_x, g.gene_y, color=c, s=50, alpha=.35, edgecolors=CREAM, label=tissue, zorder=3)
    m, b = np.polyfit(co.gene_x, co.gene_y, 1)
    xs = np.array([co.gene_x.min(), co.gene_x.max()])
    ax.plot(xs, m * xs + b, color=RED, lw=2.2, zorder=1)
    ax.xaxis.grid(False)
    co["resid"] = co.gene_y - (m * co.gene_x + b)
    hot = co.loc[co.resid.idxmax()]
    ax.annotate(f"{hot.tissue} outlier", xy=(hot.gene_x, hot.gene_y),
                xytext=(hot.gene_x - 3.2, hot.gene_y + 2.0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=INK, lw=1.6,
                                connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.3"))
    ax.scatter(hot.gene_x, hot.gene_y, s=120, color=pal[hot.tissue],
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=2.2, zorder=5)
    ax.text(0.0, 1.13, "Two genes, one trend",                       # main title
            transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    ax.text(0.0, 1.05, "co-expression across three tissues",         # italic subtitle
            transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, color=MUTED, style="italic")
    fig.text(0.5, -0.04, "Source: load_coexpression() · demo data",  # caption
             ha="center", fontsize=8, color=MUTED)
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right")
plt.show()

The bottom line Build in layers, then refine with properties: transparency for density, a lighter grid, a curved arrow plus a white edge to single one point out, and a layered title / subtitle / caption to say what it means.

Exercise — Load, Scatter, Correlate

Exercise · your turn

Your turn: run the whole recipe on a new dataset

load_scatter_demo() is a synthetic practice dataset (log2fc, expression, group). Load it, scatter expression against log2fc, then compute Pearson r and print it in the corner. Use the house style from Step 5.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_scatter_demo

df = load_scatter_demo()        # columns: log2fc, expression, group

# 1. make a figure + axes
# 2. scatter expression (y) against log2fc (x)
# 3. r = np.corrcoef(...)  ->  ax.text(...) it in the top-left
# 4. label the axes
# your code here

Exercise Get the mechanics working first: load → scatter → annotate r. We’ll look at what the number actually means on the next slide.

Exercise — Solution & the Catch

Exercise · solution

r is high — but here that is an artifact

The recipe runs and prints a strong-looking r. The catch: in this toy dataset expression was built as 0.8 * log2fc + noise, so the correlation is baked in, and group is assigned at random. The number is real; the biology is not. Always ask what generated the data before trusting an r.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_scatter_demo

df = load_scatter_demo()

with plt.rc_context(house):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.6))
    ax.scatter(df.log2fc, df.expression, color=GREY, s=45, alpha=.7)
    r = np.corrcoef(df.log2fc, df.expression)[0, 1]   # Pearson r
    ax.text(0.04, 0.93, f"r = {r:.2f}", transform=ax.transAxes,
            fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=INK)
    ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change")
    ax.set_ylabel("expression")
plt.show()

Exercise · the lesson A high r only means two columns move together. Here they move together by construction. Correlation is a description, not a discovery.

Ternary Plots

Compositional data · three parts that sum to one

Ternary · The Data

Genomics · compositional data

Three ancestry fractions per individual, summing to one

Each individual’s ancestry splits across three populations and the fractions sum to 1. We simulate that with a Dirichlet draw: mostly-A, mostly-B, mostly-C, plus some evenly admixed.

import numpy as np, pandas as pd

rng_adm = np.random.default_rng(7)
comp = np.vstack([rng_adm.dirichlet(a, n) for a, n in
                  [([8,1,1], 30), ([1,8,1], 30), ([1,1,8], 30), ([2,2,2], 20)]])
adm = pd.DataFrame(comp, columns=["Pop A", "Pop B", "Pop C"]).round(3)
adm.head(4)
Pop A Pop B Pop C
0 0.840 0.062 0.098
1 0.697 0.001 0.302
2 0.882 0.075 0.043
3 0.791 0.187 0.022

Ternary · Step 1 — The Triangle

Genomics · compositional data

1 · Frame

ternary_diagram draws the triangle, gridlines, and ticks for you. Three corners, one per population. Near a corner means mostly that population, the centre means evenly admixed.

from ternary_diagram import TernaryDiagram

rng_adm = np.random.default_rng(7)        # fixed seed -> same points every step
comp = np.vstack([rng_adm.dirichlet(a, n) for a, n in
                  [([8,1,1], 30), ([1,8,1], 30), ([1,1,8], 30), ([2,2,2], 20)]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
td = TernaryDiagram(["Pop A", "Pop B", "Pop C"], ax=ax)   # frame, gridlines, ticks
plt.show()

Ternary · Step 2 — The Points

Genomics · compositional data

2 · Scatter

td.scatter takes the whole comp array, one row per individual. It places each point by its three fractions automatically. One colour for now.

from ternary_diagram import TernaryDiagram

rng_adm = np.random.default_rng(7)
comp = np.vstack([rng_adm.dirichlet(a, n) for a, n in
                  [([8,1,1], 30), ([1,8,1], 30), ([1,1,8], 30), ([2,2,2], 20)]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
td = TernaryDiagram(["Pop A", "Pop B", "Pop C"], ax=ax)
td.scatter(vector=comp, c=GREY, s=28, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=0.4, zorder=3)   # one dot per individual
plt.show()

Ternary · Step 3 — Colour by Population

Genomics · compositional data

3 · Colour

Colour each point by its dominant population (argmax of the three fractions). The three corner clusters light up; the admixed individuals stay near the middle.

from ternary_diagram import TernaryDiagram

rng_adm = np.random.default_rng(7)
comp = np.vstack([rng_adm.dirichlet(a, n) for a, n in
                  [([8,1,1], 30), ([1,8,1], 30), ([1,1,8], 30), ([2,2,2], 20)]])

cols = np.array([GREEN, BLUE, AMBER])[comp.argmax(1)]   # colour by dominant population
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
td = TernaryDiagram(["Pop A", "Pop B", "Pop C"], ax=ax)
td.scatter(vector=comp, c=cols, s=28, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=0.4, zorder=3)
plt.show()

The bottom line Three parts that sum to one belong in a triangle. Corners are pure ancestry, the centre is admixture, and argmax colouring reveals the dominant population at a glance.

ternary-diagram (yu9824), MIT. Install: pip install ternary-diagram.

Volcano Plots

Differential expression · Day 01

What Is a Volcano Plot?

Differential expression · theory

Effect size meets significance

A volcano plot answers two questions at once for every gene: how much did it change, and how sure are we. Each dot is one gene.

The x-axis is log2 fold change, the size and direction of the change. The y-axis is −log10(p-value), so higher means more significant. Genes pile up along the bottom (no change, not significant) and the interesting ones rise into the top corners.

Two thresholds carve out the hits: a fold-change cutoff (typically |log2FC| > 1, a two-fold change) and a significance cutoff (p < 0.05, i.e. −log10 p > 1.3). Top-right is up-regulated and significant, top-left is down-regulated and significant, everything else is background.

Anatomy of a Volcano

Differential expression · theory

The three regions, before any data

Volcano · The Data

Differential expression

Real DESeq2 output, not simulated

load_deseq2() returns one row per gene from a drought-vs-control contrast: effect size (log2FoldChange), raw and adjusted p-values (pvalue, padj), and mean expression (baseMean).

from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")   # gene, baseMean, log2FoldChange, pvalue, padj
de.head(4)
gene baseMean log2FoldChange pvalue padj
0 Gene_00000 2878.659834 0.965552 0.072316 0.999941
1 Gene_00001 2637.606836 0.457506 0.395939 0.999941
2 Gene_00002 1754.258523 1.002372 0.067253 0.999941
3 Gene_00003 11.111826 0.037154 0.973055 0.999941

Volcano · Step 1 — Effect vs Significance

Differential expression

1 · The cloud

Derive the significance axis (−log10 of the p-value) and scatter every gene. The volcano shape appears: a wide base of unchanged genes, two rising arms.

from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")              # one row per gene
de["neg_log10_p"] = -np.log10(de.pvalue)          # significance axis

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.8))
ax.scatter(de.log2FoldChange, de.neg_log10_p, color=GREY, s=8, alpha=.4, linewidths=0)
ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change")
ax.set_ylabel("-log10(p)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Volcano · Step 2 — Classify & Colour

Differential expression

2 · Direction

Label each gene up / down / ns from its fold change and adjusted p-value, then colour by that label. Red up, green down, grey for the background.

from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")
de["neg_log10_p"] = -np.log10(de.pvalue)
de["reg"] = np.where((de.log2FoldChange >  1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "up",     # classify
            np.where((de.log2FoldChange < -1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "down", "ns"))

cm = {"up": RED, "down": GREEN, "ns": GREY}        # red up, green down, grey ns
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.8))
for st, grp in de.groupby("reg"):
    ax.scatter(grp.log2FoldChange, grp.neg_log10_p, c=cm[st],
               s=26 if st != "ns" else 7, alpha=.75 if st != "ns" else .3,
               linewidths=0, zorder=3 if st != "ns" else 1)
ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change")
ax.set_ylabel("-log10(p)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Volcano · Step 3 — Threshold Lines

Differential expression

3 · Cutoffs

Draw the cutoffs that define the call: a horizontal line at p = 0.05 and vertical lines at ±1 log2FC. Now the colour regions have visible borders.

from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")
de["neg_log10_p"] = -np.log10(de.pvalue)
de["reg"] = np.where((de.log2FoldChange >  1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "up",
            np.where((de.log2FoldChange < -1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "down", "ns"))

cm = {"up": RED, "down": GREEN, "ns": GREY}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.8))
for st, grp in de.groupby("reg"):
    ax.scatter(grp.log2FoldChange, grp.neg_log10_p, c=cm[st],
               s=26 if st != "ns" else 7, alpha=.75 if st != "ns" else .3,
               linewidths=0, zorder=3 if st != "ns" else 1)
ax.axhline(-np.log10(0.05), color=INK, lw=.8, ls="--")   # significance cutoff p=0.05
ax.axvline( 1, color=INK, lw=.8, ls="--")                # fold-change cutoffs
ax.axvline(-1, color=INK, lw=.8, ls="--")
ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change")
ax.set_ylabel("-log10(p)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Volcano · Step 4 — Label the Top Genes

Differential expression

4 · Annotate

Take the most significant hits, label them, and let adjustText nudge the labels apart so they don’t overlap. The title states the count.

from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2
from adjustText import adjust_text            # nudges labels apart

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")
de["neg_log10_p"] = -np.log10(de.pvalue)
de["reg"] = np.where((de.log2FoldChange >  1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "up",
            np.where((de.log2FoldChange < -1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "down", "ns"))

cm = {"up": RED, "down": GREEN, "ns": GREY}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.8, 4.8))
for st, grp in de.groupby("reg"):
    ax.scatter(grp.log2FoldChange, grp.neg_log10_p, c=cm[st],
               s=26 if st != "ns" else 7, alpha=.75 if st != "ns" else .3,
               linewidths=0, zorder=3 if st != "ns" else 1)
ax.axhline(-np.log10(0.05), color=INK, lw=.8, ls="--")
ax.axvline( 1, color=INK, lw=.8, ls="--")
ax.axvline(-1, color=INK, lw=.8, ls="--")
top = de[de.reg != "ns"].nsmallest(8, "pvalue")        # 8 most significant
texts = [ax.text(r.log2FoldChange, r.neg_log10_p, r.gene, fontsize=6, fontweight="bold")
         for _, r in top.iterrows()]
adjust_text(texts, ax=ax, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=GREY, lw=.6))   # de-overlap
ax.set_xlabel("log2 fold change")
ax.set_ylabel("-log10(p)")
ax.set_title(f"Drought DE: {(de.reg=='up').sum()} up, {(de.reg=='down').sum()} down", color="#333333")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

The bottom line A volcano puts effect size (x) against significance (y). Classify, colour by direction (red up, green down, grey background), draw the threshold lines, and label the top hits. On the real drought contrast that’s ~100 up and ~118 down.

Interactive Volcano

Differential expression · Plotly

From Static to Interactive

Differential expression · Plotly

Same data, now you can hover and zoom

The matplotlib volcano is perfect for print. For exploration you want hover to read the gene, zoom into a cluster, and toggle a class on and off. Plotly gives all three from the same DataFrame, and the figure embeds live in the slide.

A note on Dash: Dash adds dropdowns, sliders, and callbacks, but it runs as its own web server and cannot live inside a slide. The interactive figure below is the part that embeds. The final slide shows the Dash wrapper for when you want the standalone app.

Plotly · Step 1 — The Scatter

Differential expression · Plotly

1 · One call

px.scatter builds the whole figure from the DataFrame. Reuse the reg and neg_log10_p columns from the matplotlib build, no new data work.

import plotly.express as px
from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")
de["neg_log10_p"] = -np.log10(de.pvalue)
de["reg"] = np.where((de.log2FoldChange >  1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "up",
            np.where((de.log2FoldChange < -1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "down", "ns"))

fig = px.scatter(de, x="log2FoldChange", y="neg_log10_p",
                 labels={"log2FoldChange": "log2 fold change",
                         "neg_log10_p": "-log10(p)"})
fig.show()

Plotly · Step 2 — Colour & Hover

Differential expression · Plotly

2 · Direction + identity

Colour by reg with the same red/green/grey map, and set hover_name so pointing at any dot reveals the gene and its p-value. This is the payoff over a static image.

import plotly.express as px
from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")
de["neg_log10_p"] = -np.log10(de.pvalue)
de["reg"] = np.where((de.log2FoldChange >  1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "up",
            np.where((de.log2FoldChange < -1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "down", "ns"))

fig = px.scatter(de, x="log2FoldChange", y="neg_log10_p", color="reg",
                 color_discrete_map={"up": RED, "down": GREEN, "ns": GREY},
                 category_orders={"reg": ["up", "down", "ns"]},
                 hover_name="gene", hover_data={"pvalue": ":.1e", "reg": False},
                 labels={"log2FoldChange": "log2 fold change", "neg_log10_p": "-log10(p)"})
fig.show()

Plotly · Step 3 — Thresholds & Polish

Differential expression · Plotly

3 · Make it look nicer

Add the cutoff lines, shrink the markers, drop a clean template, and let the cream slide show through with a transparent background. Now it matches the deck.

import plotly.express as px
from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")
de["neg_log10_p"] = -np.log10(de.pvalue)
de["reg"] = np.where((de.log2FoldChange >  1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "up",
            np.where((de.log2FoldChange < -1) & (de.padj < 0.05), "down", "ns"))

fig = px.scatter(de, x="log2FoldChange", y="neg_log10_p", color="reg",
                 color_discrete_map={"up": RED, "down": GREEN, "ns": GREY},
                 category_orders={"reg": ["up", "down", "ns"]},
                 hover_name="gene", hover_data={"pvalue": ":.1e", "reg": False},
                 labels={"log2FoldChange": "log2 fold change", "neg_log10_p": "-log10(p)"})
fig.add_hline(y=-np.log10(0.05), line_dash="dash", line_color=INK, line_width=1)
fig.add_vline(x=1,  line_dash="dash", line_color=INK, line_width=1)
fig.add_vline(x=-1, line_dash="dash", line_color=INK, line_width=1)
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=5, opacity=0.6, line=dict(width=0)))
fig.update_layout(template="simple_white", height=440,
                  paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
                  font=dict(family="Asap", color=INK, size=12),
                  legend_title_text="", margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=30, b=10))
fig.show()

The bottom line Plotly turns the same DataFrame into an explorable volcano: hover for the gene, zoom into a cluster, click the legend to isolate a class. One px.scatter, a colour map, threshold lines, and a transparent template to match the deck.

Wrapping It in a Dash App

Differential expression · Plotly

For a standalone, deployable tool (runs as its own server)

Dash adds controls and callbacks, a p-value slider that re-filters the volcano live. This can’t run inside a slide; save it as app.py and run python app.py.

from dash import Dash, dcc, html, Input, Output
import plotly.express as px
from genomics_course.data import load_deseq2

de = load_deseq2(contrast="drought")
de["neg_log10_p"] = -np.log10(de.pvalue)

app = Dash(__name__)
app.layout = html.Div([
    html.H3("Volcano explorer"),
    dcc.Slider(0, 5, 0.5, value=1.3, id="p-cut"),   # significance slider
    dcc.Graph(id="volcano"),
])

@app.callback(Output("volcano", "figure"), Input("p-cut", "value"))
def draw(p_cut):
    d = de.copy()
    d["reg"] = np.where((d.log2FoldChange >  1) & (d.neg_log10_p > p_cut), "up",
               np.where((d.log2FoldChange < -1) & (d.neg_log10_p > p_cut), "down", "ns"))
    fig = px.scatter(d, x="log2FoldChange", y="neg_log10_p", color="reg",
                     color_discrete_map={"up": RED, "down": GREEN, "ns": GREY},
                     hover_name="gene")
    fig.add_hline(y=p_cut, line_dash="dash")
    return fig

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run(debug=True)   # opens http://127.0.0.1:8050

Dimensionality Reduction

Many features into two axes · Day 01

Why Reduce, and Which Method

Dimensionality reduction · theory

Three projections, three jobs

Genomic data is wide: thousands of genes, hundreds of samples. You can’t see 5000 dimensions, so you project to two while keeping what matters. The three standard tools keep different things, so they answer different questions.

Method Keeps Speed Best genomics use
PCA Global variance, real distances, interpretable axes Fast Population structure from genotypes/ancestry; bulk RNA-seq QC; batch detection
t-SNE Local neighbourhoods (tight clusters) Slow Single-cell RNA-seq cluster visualisation
UMAP Local + some global; reproducible Fast Single-cell (the scanpy default); large datasets

The rule of thumb: PCA to understand structure and distances, t-SNE / UMAP to see clusters.

The Three Rules That Save You

Dimensionality reduction · theory

Before you trust an embedding

PCA is linear; t-SNE and UMAP are not. PCA axes are combinations of features you can interpret and whose distances are real. In t-SNE and UMAP, distances between clusters carry no meaning, only “these points are neighbours.”

Run t-SNE / UMAP on PCA-reduced data. For thousands of genes, reduce to ~50 PCs first, then embed. It is faster and denoises. (Our ancestry data is already 5-dimensional, so we skip that here.)

Seed everything. t-SNE and UMAP are stochastic; set random_state or the picture changes every run.

Dim. Reduction · The Data

Dimensionality reduction

Real ancestry: 120 individuals, 5 populations

load_admixture() gives each individual’s ancestry split across five source populations (K1–K5, summing to 1) plus the population label. This is the textbook home of PCA in genomics: revealing population structure.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()   # individual, population, K1..K5
adm.head(4)
individual population K1 K2 K3 K4 K5
0 EUR_000 EUR 0.978699 0.002754 0.000058 0.000306 1.818301e-02
1 EUR_001 EUR 0.978085 0.011594 0.000160 0.001027 9.134997e-03
2 EUR_002 EUR 0.977956 0.009453 0.000056 0.009910 2.624863e-03
3 EUR_003 EUR 0.971030 0.001839 0.025570 0.001560 4.514676e-07

PCA · Step 1 — Project

Dimensionality reduction · PCA

1 · Scale, fit, plot

Scale each feature, fit PCA, and scatter the first two components. Structure is already visible, but we can’t yet tell which cluster is which.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)            # centre + scale each feature
pca = PCA(n_components=5, random_state=42)
coords = pca.fit_transform(Xs)                    # project onto components

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
ax.scatter(coords[:, 0], coords[:, 1], color=GREY, s=24, alpha=.7, linewidths=0)
ax.set_xlabel("PC1"); ax.set_ylabel("PC2")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

PCA · Step 2 — Colour by Population

Dimensionality reduction · PCA

2 · Structure appears

Colour by population and add the variance each axis explains. The five groups separate, and PCA’s real distances show AMR sitting between the others, it is the admixed population.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
pca = PCA(n_components=5, random_state=42)
coords = pca.fit_transform(Xs)
var = pca.explained_variance_ratio_ * 100         # % variance per PC
pal = {"EUR": GREEN, "AFR": BLUE, "EAS": AMBER, "SAS": RED, "AMR": PURPLE}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
for p, c in pal.items():
    m = adm.population == p
    ax.scatter(coords[m, 0], coords[m, 1], color=c, s=24, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=.3, label=p)
ax.set_xlabel(f"PC1 ({var[0]:.0f}%)"); ax.set_ylabel(f"PC2 ({var[1]:.0f}%)")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9, title="population")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

PCA · How Many Components?

Dimensionality reduction · PCA

The scree plot, and a compositional quirk

The scree plot shows variance per component. Normally you look for an “elbow.” Here you get four near-equal components and a fifth at zero: because the five fractions sum to 1, the data really lives in four dimensions.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
pca = PCA(n_components=5, random_state=42).fit(Xs)
var = pca.explained_variance_ratio_ * 100
cum = var.cumsum()                                # cumulative variance

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
pcs = range(1, 6)
ax.bar(pcs, var, color=GREEN, alpha=.85, edgecolor="white")   # per-PC variance
ax.plot(pcs, cum, color=INK, marker="o", lw=1.5)              # cumulative
ax.set_xlabel("principal component"); ax.set_ylabel("variance explained (%)")
ax.set_title("4 even PCs, PC5 ≈ 0 (fractions sum to 1)", color="#333333")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

t-SNE · Local Clusters

Dimensionality reduction · t-SNE

Same data, tightened into clusters

t-SNE drops the linear constraint and pulls neighbours together. The populations become tight, well-separated blobs, great for spotting clusters, but the gaps between them mean nothing.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
emb = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, init="pca", random_state=42).fit_transform(Xs)

pal = {"EUR": GREEN, "AFR": BLUE, "EAS": AMBER, "SAS": RED, "AMR": PURPLE}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
for p, c in pal.items():
    m = adm.population == p
    ax.scatter(emb[m, 0], emb[m, 1], color=c, s=24, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=.3, label=p)
ax.set_xlabel("t-SNE 1"); ax.set_ylabel("t-SNE 2")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

UMAP · Local + Some Global

Dimensionality reduction · UMAP

Faster, reproducible, the single-cell default

UMAP keeps tight clusters like t-SNE but runs faster and preserves a little more of the global layout. n_neighbors trades local detail for global structure; min_dist controls how tightly points pack.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import umap

adm = load_admixture()
X = adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
emb = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, random_state=42).fit_transform(Xs)

pal = {"EUR": GREEN, "AFR": BLUE, "EAS": AMBER, "SAS": RED, "AMR": PURPLE}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 4.6))
for p, c in pal.items():
    m = adm.population == p
    ax.scatter(emb[m, 0], emb[m, 1], color=c, s=24, alpha=.8, edgecolors=CREAM, linewidths=.3, label=p)
ax.set_xlabel("UMAP 1"); ax.set_ylabel("UMAP 2")
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=9)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Side by Side

Dimensionality reduction

Same ancestry data, three projections

The bottom line PCA keeps real distances and interpretable axes, reach for it first and for population structure. t-SNE and UMAP trade distance for crisp clusters, reach for them on single-cell. Same five populations here, three different lenses.

UMAP Is a Network

Dimensionality reduction · UMAP

The embedding is a neighbour graph laid flat

UMAP works in two moves: first it builds a weighted k-nearest-neighbour graph (who is close to whom), then it lays that graph out in 2D. umap.plot.connectivity draws the graph itself, points plus the edges. Dense clumps are the populations (everyone is everyone’s neighbour); the thin threads between clumps are the handful of cross-population links. Seeing the graph explains why UMAP clusters: it is a network embedding, not a projection.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import umap, umap.plot

adm = load_admixture()
Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(adm[["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]].values)

reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, random_state=42).fit(Xs)   # .fit keeps the model
umap.plot.connectivity(reducer, show_points=True)   # draw the neighbour graph

The bottom line UMAP first builds a kNN graph, then embeds it. connectivity shows that graph directly: tight knots are clusters, thin bridges are the rare links between them. The 2D scatter you usually see is just this network, flattened.

from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression   # course loader, real values

te

Bar · Step 1 — Plain Bars

Bar charts · build

1 · Default matplotlib

Sort low-to-high so the largest bar ends on top, then draw. Functional, but every bar shouts equally and the frame is noisy.

from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")   # sort so the biggest bar ends on top

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))         # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm)                          # horizontal bars, default colour
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                 # start at 0 so bar length == value
plt.show()

Bar · Step 2 — Colour Carries the Story

Bar charts · build

2 · One bold, the rest quiet

Build a colour list: red for Heart, grey for everything else. The eye lands on the one bar that matters before reading a single label.

from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")              # tissue, tpm; sorted
colors = [RED if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te.tissue]   # one bold colour, rest grey

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))                    # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=colors)                      # apply the per-bar colours
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                           # zero baseline
plt.show()

Bar · Step 3 — Drop the Frame

Bar charts · build

3 · Less ink

Hide the left, right, and top spines and the y-ticks, then add a faint grid on the x-axis only. Only the scale that matters survives.

from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")              # tissue, tpm; sorted
colors = [RED if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te.tissue]   # one bold, rest grey

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))                    # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=colors)                      # coloured bars
for s in ["left", "right", "top"]:                            # walk the three unwanted spines
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)                           # remove each one
ax.tick_params(left=False)                                    # drop the y-axis tick marks
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=.3, lw=.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)    # faint x grid, behind the bars
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                           # zero baseline
plt.show()

Bar · Step 4 — Label the Bars

Bar charts · build

4 · Values on the bars

ax.bar_label writes each value at the end of its bar. Now the reader gets the exact number without chasing a gridline.

from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")              # tissue, tpm; sorted
colors = [RED if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te.tissue]   # one bold, rest grey

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))                    # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=colors)                      # coloured bars
for s in ["left", "right", "top"]:                            # remove unwanted spines
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(left=False)                                    # no y ticks
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=.3, lw=.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)    # faint x grid behind bars
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], padding=6, color=INK, fontsize=10)  # value at the end of each bar
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                           # zero baseline
plt.show()

Bar · Step 5 — Say What It Shows

Bar charts · build

5 · A descriptive title

A title that states the finding, not the variables. “BRCA1 is highest in heart tissue” does the interpreting for the reader; a subtitle gives the units.

from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression().sort_values("tpm")              # tissue, tpm; sorted
colors = [RED if t == "Heart" else GREY for t in te.tissue]   # one bold, rest grey

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 4.4))                    # one panel
ax.barh(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=colors)                      # coloured bars
for s in ["left", "right", "top"]:                            # remove unwanted spines
    ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(left=False)                                    # no y ticks
ax.grid(axis="x", alpha=.3, lw=.6); ax.set_axisbelow(True)    # faint x grid behind bars
ax.bar_label(ax.containers[0], padding=6, color=INK, fontsize=10)  # value labels
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)                                           # zero baseline
fig.suptitle("BRCA1 is highest in heart tissue", fontsize=13, fontweight="bold",   # finding, not variables
             color=INK, x=.04, ha="left", y=.98)              # pin it left, near the top
fig.text(.04, .90, "Expression across five tissues (TPM)", fontsize=10, color=MUTED)  # subtitle = units
plt.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, .88])                         # leave headroom for the two-line header
plt.show()

The bottom line Colour carries the story. Spend the loud colour on the row that matters; frame, ticks, and legend disappear. The recipe: sort → one bold colour → drop the frame → label the bars → title the finding.

Stacked Bars · Composition Over Time

Metagenomics · theory

Watch the whole shift, day by day

A stacked bar shows composition: each bar is a whole (one sample) split into parts (taxa) that sum to 1. Line the bars up along time and you don’t just compare samples, you watch the community change: a perturbation hits, one taxon blooms, the rest recover.

Two rules keep it readable: keep the taxon order and colours identical across every bar, so a band means the same thing on day 1 and day 16, and mark the event (here, antibiotics) so the cause sits next to the effect. Microbiome tables arrive tidy/long, so the first move is a pivot to wide.

Stacked Bars · The Data

Metagenomics

Daily phylum abundance across an antibiotic course

load_microbiome() returns tidy long form: one row per day-taxon, abundances summing to 1 each day, with a phase label (baseline / antibiotic / recovery).

from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()           # day, phase, taxon, abundance
mb.head(4)
day phase taxon abundance
0 1 baseline Firmicutes 0.423255
1 1 baseline Bacteroidetes 0.360016
2 1 baseline Proteobacteria 0.040348
3 1 baseline Actinobacteria 0.073075

Stacked Bars · Step 1 — Pivot & Stack

Metagenomics · build

1 · Long to wide, stacked along time

Pivot to one row per day, one column per taxon, then stack the taxa with a running bottom. The x-axis is time, so the bloom is already visible mid-course.

from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                            # long: day, phase, taxon, abundance
wide = mb.pivot(index="day", columns="taxon", values="abundance") # rows = days, columns = taxa
taxa = ["Firmicutes", "Bacteroidetes", "Proteobacteria",         # fixed taxon order for now
        "Actinobacteria", "Verrucomicrobia", "Other"]
tax_pal = {"Firmicutes": GREEN, "Bacteroidetes": BLUE,           # one fixed colour per taxon
           "Proteobacteria": RED, "Actinobacteria": AMBER,
           "Verrucomicrobia": PURPLE, "Other": GREY}
days = wide.index.values                                         # x positions = the days

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))                       # one panel
bottom = np.zeros(len(wide))                                     # running base height of the stack
for t in taxa:                                                   # add one taxon layer at a time
    ax.bar(days, wide[t], bottom=bottom, color=tax_pal[t],       # this taxon's slice of each day
           width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=t)                      # width 1 so days touch into a band
    bottom += wide[t].values                                     # raise base for the next layer
ax.set_xlim(days.min() - 0.5, days.max() + 0.5)                  # tight x range
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)                                                # composition fills 0–1
ax.set_xlabel("day"); ax.set_ylabel("relative abundance")
plt.show()

Stacked Bars · Step 2 — Order by Abundance

Metagenomics · build

2 · Most abundant at the bottom

Replace the fixed taxon list with one sorted by mean abundance. The dominant phyla anchor the base of every bar; rare ones ride on top, the convention that makes the stack legible.

from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
wide = mb.pivot(index="day", columns="taxon", values="abundance")  # days × taxa
taxa = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # mean abundance of each taxon...
          .sort_values(ascending=False).index)                  # ...most abundant first → stack bottom
tax_pal = {"Firmicutes": GREEN, "Bacteroidetes": BLUE,          # fixed colour per taxon
           "Proteobacteria": RED, "Actinobacteria": AMBER,
           "Verrucomicrobia": PURPLE, "Other": GREY}
days = wide.index.values                                         # days on x

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))                       # one panel
bottom = np.zeros(len(wide))                                     # running base
for t in taxa:                                                  # layer in abundance order now
    ax.bar(days, wide[t], bottom=bottom, color=tax_pal[t],
           width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=t)
    bottom += wide[t].values                                     # raise base
ax.set_xlim(days.min() - 0.5, days.max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("day"); ax.set_ylabel("relative abundance")
plt.show()

Stacked Bars · Step 3 — Mark the Event

Metagenomics · build

3 · Put the cause next to the effect

Shade the antibiotic window and label it. Now the Proteobacteria swell sits directly under its trigger, the bloom reads as a consequence, not a coincidence.

from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
wide = mb.pivot(index="day", columns="taxon", values="abundance")  # days × taxa
taxa = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # taxa, most abundant first
          .sort_values(ascending=False).index)
tax_pal = {"Firmicutes": GREEN, "Bacteroidetes": BLUE,          # fixed colour per taxon
           "Proteobacteria": RED, "Actinobacteria": AMBER,
           "Verrucomicrobia": PURPLE, "Other": GREY}
days = wide.index.values

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))
bottom = np.zeros(len(wide))
for t in taxa:                                                  # stack the taxa
    ax.bar(days, wide[t], bottom=bottom, color=tax_pal[t],
           width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=t)
    bottom += wide[t].values
ax.axvspan(4.5, 7.5, color=INK, alpha=.06)                       # shade the antibiotic window (days 5–7)
ax.text(6, 0.94, "antibiotics", ha="center", color=INK, fontsize=9)  # name the perturbation
ax.set_xlim(days.min() - 0.5, days.max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("day"); ax.set_ylabel("relative abundance")
plt.show()

Stacked Bars · Step 4 — Percent Axis & Finding

Metagenomics · build

4 · Name the result

Add the taxon legend, a percent y-axis, and a title that states the biology. The story reads in one glance: bloom under antibiotics, recovery after.

import matplotlib.ticker as mtick                                # percent-axis formatter
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
wide = mb.pivot(index="day", columns="taxon", values="abundance")  # days × taxa
taxa = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # taxa, most abundant first
          .sort_values(ascending=False).index)
tax_pal = {"Firmicutes": GREEN, "Bacteroidetes": BLUE,          # fixed colour per taxon
           "Proteobacteria": RED, "Actinobacteria": AMBER,
           "Verrucomicrobia": PURPLE, "Other": GREY}
days = wide.index.values

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.8, 4.4))
bottom = np.zeros(len(wide))
for t in taxa:                                                  # stack the taxa
    ax.bar(days, wide[t], bottom=bottom, color=tax_pal[t],
           width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=t)
    bottom += wide[t].values
ax.axvspan(4.5, 7.5, color=INK, alpha=.06)                       # antibiotic window
ax.text(6, 0.94, "antibiotics", ha="center", color=INK, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(days.min() - 0.5, days.max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_yticks([0, .5, 1])                    # clean 0 / 50 / 100 ticks
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mtick.PercentFormatter(1, decimals=0))  # render 0–1 as 0–100%
ax.set_xlabel("day"); ax.set_ylabel("relative abundance")
ax.set_title("ANTIBIOTICS TRIGGER A PROTEOBACTERIA BLOOM",       # title = the finding
             color="#333333", fontweight="bold", loc="left")
ax.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1), loc="upper left",            # taxon key, outside right
          frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.show()

The bottom line Along time, a stacked bar shows the community moving: pivot to days×taxa → order taxa by abundance → mark the event → percent axis + finding. Fixed colours and band order let the eye track one taxon across the whole course, the Proteobacteria bloom rises under antibiotics and fades in recovery.

Treemap · The Data

Composition · treemap

Collapse time to one community

The stacked bar showed every day. Average across them and you get the whole community as one set of parts, exactly what a treemap wants.

from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                          # day, phase, taxon, abundance
comm = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                    # mean abundance across all days
          .sort_values(ascending=False).reset_index())         # biggest first
comm["pct"] = comm.abundance * 100                             # as a percentage for labels
comm

Treemap · Step 1 — Tile by Value

Composition · build

1 · squarify

squarify.plot takes sizes and labels and tiles them largest-first. pad=True leaves thin gaps so tiles read as separate. Turn the axis off, it’s a canvas, not a plot.

import squarify                                                  # the treemap layout library
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
comm = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # community = mean over all days
          .sort_values(ascending=False).reset_index())          # biggest first (squarify expects sorted)
comm["pct"] = comm.abundance * 100                              # percentages for the labels
labels = [f"{t}\n{p:.0f}%" for t, p in zip(comm.taxon, comm.pct)]  # "Firmicutes\n33%" per tile

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0)); ax.set_axis_off()   # blank canvas, no axes
squarify.plot(sizes=comm.abundance, label=labels, pad=True,     # tile area == abundance
              color=[GREEN, BLUE, RED, AMBER, PURPLE, GREY], ax=ax)  # explicit taxon colours
plt.show()

Treemap · Step 2 — Palette from pypalettes

Composition · build

2 · Borrow a curated palette

pypalettes ships hundreds of named palettes. load_cmap fetches one; pd.factorize turns the category column into colour indices, so each taxon gets its own swatch. White label text reads cleanly on the darker tiles.

import squarify
from pypalettes import load_cmap                                 # curated palette library
from genomics_course.data import load_microbiome

mb = load_microbiome()                                           # long form
comm = (mb.groupby("taxon").abundance.mean()                     # community mean over days
          .sort_values(ascending=False).reset_index())
comm["pct"] = comm.abundance * 100                              # percentages
labels = [f"{t}\n{p:.0f}%" for t, p in zip(comm.taxon, comm.pct)]  # tile labels

cmap = load_cmap("Acadia")                                       # any named palette (discrete cmap)
codes, _ = pd.factorize(comm.taxon)                              # taxon → integer index 0,1,2,...
colors = [cmap(c) for c in codes]                                # one palette colour per taxon

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0)); ax.set_axis_off()   # blank canvas
squarify.plot(sizes=comm.abundance, label=labels, color=colors, pad=True,  # tiles in palette colours
              text_kwargs={"color": "white", "fontsize": 10}, ax=ax)       # white labels on the tiles
plt.show()

The bottom line A treemap shows part-to-whole when there are too many parts for a bar or pie. squarify tiles a flat set, sized by value; style it with any pypalettes colormap. Label the tiles, areas are read approximately, not precisely.

Admixture · The Data

Population structure

One row per individual, ancestry split across K populations

load_admixture() returns each individual’s inferred ancestry across five source populations (K1–K5, summing to 1) plus its assigned population. An admixture plot turns each row into one stacked bar.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()   # individual, population, K1..K5
adm.head(4)
individual population K1 K2 K3 K4 K5
0 EUR_000 EUR 0.978699 0.002754 0.000058 0.000306 1.818301e-02
1 EUR_001 EUR 0.978085 0.011594 0.000160 0.001027 9.134997e-03
2 EUR_002 EUR 0.977956 0.009453 0.000056 0.009910 2.624863e-03
3 EUR_003 EUR 0.971030 0.001839 0.025570 0.001560 4.514676e-07

Admixture · Step 1 — Stack the Components

Population structure · build

1 · Stacked bars

One bar per individual, each K segment stacked on the last via a running bottom. With width=1.0 and linewidth=0 the bars touch into a solid block. Within each population the order is still random, so it looks noisy.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)  # shuffle within pops so sorting later has an effect
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # the five ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # one colour per ancestry

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))             # x = individuals, running stack base
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack one K component at a time
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)  # this K's slice
    bottom += adm[col].values                                     # raise base for the next K
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)             # tight x, full 0–1 height
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
plt.show()

Admixture · Step 2 — Sort Within Population

Population structure · build

2 · Order

For each population, find its dominant ancestry and sort its individuals by that column. The noise resolves into a clean gradient, the single most important step for a readable admixture plot.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)  # grouped by pop, shuffled within
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # ancestry colours

parts = []                                                        # collect each sorted population block
for p in adm.population.drop_duplicates():                        # for each population, in order
    block = adm[adm.population == p]                              # just that population's individuals
    dom = block[Kc].mean().idxmax()                              # its dominant ancestry column
    parts.append(block.sort_values(dom, ascending=False))        # sort individuals by that ancestry
adm = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)                        # stitch the sorted blocks back together

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))             # x = individuals, stack base
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack the K components
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)
    bottom += adm[col].values                                     # raise base
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
plt.show()

Admixture · Step 3 — Separate the Populations

Population structure · build

3 · White lines

Find where one population ends and the next begins (cumulative group sizes) and draw a thin white line at each boundary. Now the five groups read as distinct blocks.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # ancestry colours

parts = []                                                        # sort within each population (as Step 2)
for p in adm.population.drop_duplicates():
    block = adm[adm.population == p]
    dom = block[Kc].mean().idxmax()
    parts.append(block.sort_values(dom, ascending=False))
adm = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)

pops = adm.population.drop_duplicates().tolist()                  # populations in plotted order
sizes = adm.population.value_counts()[pops].values               # how many individuals in each
bounds = np.cumsum(sizes)                                         # cumulative edges between populations

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack the K components
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)
    bottom += adm[col].values
for b in bounds[:-1]:                                             # at every internal boundary...
    ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color="white", lw=2.2)                   # ...draw a white separator
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
plt.show()

Admixture · Step 4 — Label & Polish

Population structure · build

4 · Read it

Put one tick at the centre of each population block, label it, add the K legend and a title. The figure now reads itself: who is mostly one ancestry, who is admixed.

from genomics_course.data import load_admixture

adm = load_admixture()                                            # individual, population, K1..K5
adm = adm.sample(frac=1, random_state=1).sort_values("population", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)
Kc = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]                               # ancestry columns
pal = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                           # ancestry colours

parts = []                                                        # sort within each population
for p in adm.population.drop_duplicates():
    block = adm[adm.population == p]
    dom = block[Kc].mean().idxmax()
    parts.append(block.sort_values(dom, ascending=False))
adm = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)

pops = adm.population.drop_duplicates().tolist()                  # population order
sizes = adm.population.value_counts()[pops].values               # block sizes
bounds = np.cumsum(sizes)                                         # cumulative boundaries

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 4.4))                        # one panel
x = np.arange(len(adm)); bottom = np.zeros(len(adm))
for k, col in enumerate(Kc):                                      # stack the K components
    ax.bar(x, adm[col], bottom=bottom, color=pal[k], width=1.0, linewidth=0, label=col)
    bottom += adm[col].values
for b in bounds[:-1]:                                             # white separators between populations
    ax.axvline(b - 0.5, color="white", lw=2.2)
ax.set_xticks(bounds - sizes / 2)                                # one tick at each block's centre
ax.set_xticklabels(pops, fontweight="bold", fontsize=9)          # label it with the population name
ax.set_xlim(-0.5, len(adm) - 0.5); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.set_yticks([0, .5, 1])
ax.set_ylabel("ancestry proportion")
ax.set_title("ADMIXTURE — K=5 ancestry components", color="#333333", fontweight="bold", loc="left")  # title
ax.legend(title="K", bbox_to_anchor=(1.01, 1), loc="upper left", frameon=False, fontsize=8)  # K colour key
plt.show()

The bottom line Each bar is one individual, each segment an ancestry fraction. The recipe: stack → sort within population → separate with white lines → label. Sorting is what turns noise into structure, AMR shows the most admixture, the rest are largely single-ancestry.
