Heatmaps

Expression matrices · Day 01

What a Heatmap Shows

Expression heatmaps · theory

Colour, clustering, annotation

A heatmap turns a matrix into a grid of coloured cells: gene × sample expression, a sample-by-sample correlation matrix, an epigenomic signal. Colour encodes the value, so the choice of map matters, diverging (e.g. RdBu_r, centred at 0) for z-scores that go both ways, sequential for one-directional quantities.

Two moves make it readable. Z-score each gene so a quietly-expressed gene and a loud one are on the same scale (colour then means “high/low for this gene”). Then cluster rows and columns so similar genes and similar samples sit together, the dendrograms reorder the matrix until the structure appears. seaborn.clustermap does both with good defaults; PyComplexHeatmap adds rich annotation tracks.

Heatmap · The Data

Expression heatmaps

A real expression matrix + its sample metadata

load_expression() is a log2 matrix, genes down the rows, samples across the columns. load_expression_meta() is the matching per-sample table (condition, batch, QC), the annotation we’ll layer on top.

from genomics_course.data import load_expression, load_expression_meta

expr = load_expression()        # 40 genes × 24 samples
meta = load_expression_meta()   # sample, condition, batch, qc
expr.iloc[:3, :4]
C01 C02 C03 C04
gene
G000 8.056462 8.033121 7.388702 8.039300
G001 8.009095 8.200648 8.748127 8.871357
G002 8.308926 8.052406 7.713790 8.060053

Heatmap · Step 1 — Z-Score & Colour

Expression heatmaps · build

1 · Put every gene on one scale

Z-score each gene (row), so colour means high or low relative to that gene’s own mean. Drop it into sns.heatmap with a diverging map centred at 0. The blocks are faintly there, but the rows and columns are still in file order.

import seaborn as sns                                       # heatmap / clustermap library
from genomics_course.data import load_expression

expr = load_expression()                                    # genes × samples (log2)
z = expr.sub(expr.mean(1), axis=0).div(expr.std(1), axis=0) # z-score each gene: mean 0, sd 1

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.0, 5.0))                  # one panel
sns.heatmap(z, cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, ax=ax,              # diverging map, white at z = 0
            cbar_kws={"label": "z-score"},                  # colourbar legend
            xticklabels=False, yticklabels=False)           # 40×24 labels would be unreadable
ax.set_xlabel("samples"); ax.set_ylabel("genes")
plt.show()

Heatmap · Step 2 — Cluster It

Expression heatmaps · build

2 · Let the structure sort itself

Swap heatmap for clustermap. It hierarchically clusters rows and columns and reorders both, adding dendrograms. Similar genes pull together, similar samples pull together, and the two modules and two conditions snap into clean blocks.

import seaborn as sns
from genomics_course.data import load_expression

expr = load_expression()                                    # genes × samples
z = expr.sub(expr.mean(1), axis=0).div(expr.std(1), axis=0) # per-gene z-score

cg = sns.clustermap(z, cmap="RdBu_r", center=0,             # cluster rows AND columns
                    figsize=(6.0, 5.5), xticklabels=False, yticklabels=False,
                    cbar_kws={"label": "z-score"})          # dendrograms added automatically
plt.show()

Heatmap · Step 3 — Annotate the Samples

Expression heatmaps · build

3 · Bring in the metadata

Map each sample’s condition to a colour and pass it as col_colors. A strip appears above the columns, so you can check that the clusters actually recover the biology, not a batch artefact.

import seaborn as sns
from genomics_course.data import load_expression, load_expression_meta

expr = load_expression()                                    # genes × samples
meta = load_expression_meta()                               # sample, condition, batch, qc
z = expr.sub(expr.mean(1), axis=0).div(expr.std(1), axis=0) # per-gene z-score

cond_pal = {"Control": BLUE, "Drought": AMBER}              # one colour per condition
col_colors = meta.set_index("sample")["condition"].map(cond_pal)  # colour for each sample column

cg = sns.clustermap(z, cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, figsize=(6.0, 5.5),
                    col_colors=col_colors,                  # condition strip above the columns
                    xticklabels=False, yticklabels=False, cbar_kws={"label": "z-score"})
plt.show()

Heatmap · Step 4 — Polish & Title

Expression heatmaps · build

4 · Slim the trees, add a key, name the finding

Thin the dendrograms, mute their colour, add a legend for the annotation strip, and title with the result. The figure now reads itself: two gene modules, cleanly split by condition.

import seaborn as sns
from matplotlib.patches import Patch                        # to build the condition legend
from genomics_course.data import load_expression, load_expression_meta

expr = load_expression()                                    # genes × samples
meta = load_expression_meta()                               # metadata
z = expr.sub(expr.mean(1), axis=0).div(expr.std(1), axis=0) # per-gene z-score

cond_pal = {"Control": BLUE, "Drought": AMBER}              # condition colours
col_colors = meta.set_index("sample")["condition"].map(cond_pal)  # per-column colour

cg = sns.clustermap(z, cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, figsize=(6.0, 5.5),
                    col_colors=col_colors, xticklabels=False, yticklabels=False,
                    cbar_kws={"label": "z-score"},
                    dendrogram_ratio=(.12, .12),            # slimmer dendrograms
                    tree_kws={"colors": MUTED, "linewidths": .6})  # muted tree lines
handles = [Patch(color=c, label=k) for k, c in cond_pal.items()]   # legend swatches
cg.ax_col_dendrogram.legend(handles=handles, ncol=2,        # put the key over the top dendrogram
                            frameon=False, loc="center", fontsize=8)
cg.fig.suptitle("Drought genes split into two modules",     # title states the finding
                fontweight="bold", color=INK, y=1.02)
plt.show()

The bottom line The recipe: z-score each gene → cluster rows and columns → annotate the samples → title the finding. Z-scoring makes genes comparable; clustering reorders the matrix until structure appears; the annotation strip proves the clusters are biology, not batch.

Level Up · PyComplexHeatmap

Expression heatmaps · advanced

Several annotation tracks at once

For publication figures with stacked tracks (categorical strips + numeric mini-barplots), PyComplexHeatmap mirrors R’s ComplexHeatmap. One HeatmapAnnotation holds every track.

# pip install PyComplexHeatmap
from PyComplexHeatmap import HeatmapAnnotation, anno_simple, anno_barplot, ClusterMapPlotter
from genomics_course.data import load_expression, load_expression_meta

expr = load_expression()
meta = load_expression_meta().set_index("sample")           # align metadata to matrix columns
z = expr.sub(expr.mean(1), axis=0).div(expr.std(1), axis=0) # per-gene z-score

col_ha = HeatmapAnnotation(                                 # one object, several stacked tracks
    Condition=anno_simple(meta["condition"],                # categorical strip
                          colors={"Control": BLUE, "Drought": AMBER}),
    Batch=anno_simple(meta["batch"]),                       # second categorical strip
    QC=anno_barplot(meta["qc"], colors=GREEN, height=12),   # numeric mini-barplot
    axis=1, verbose=0)

ClusterMapPlotter(data=z, top_annotation=col_ha, cmap="RdBu_r",  # clustered heatmap + tracks
                  row_cluster=True, col_cluster=True, label="z-score",
                  show_rownames=False, show_colnames=False)

Exercise · Sample QC

Expression heatmaps · exercise

Did the replicates behave?

Real scenario Before trusting any analysis, check that replicates agree and nothing is mislabelled. Build a sample × sample correlation heatmap, annotate it by condition, and read whether the two groups form clean blocks, or whether a sample sits in the wrong one (a possible swap).

import seaborn as sns
from genomics_course.data import load_expression, load_expression_meta

expr = load_expression()
meta = load_expression_meta()

# 1. corr = expr.corr()                                    # sample × sample Pearson matrix
# 2. col  = meta.set_index("sample")["condition"].map({"Control": BLUE, "Drought": AMBER})
# 3. sns.clustermap(corr, cmap="rocket", row_colors=col, col_colors=col)
# 4. read it: two clean blocks? any sample correlating with the wrong group?

Exercise · Top Variable Genes

Expression heatmaps · exercise

You can’t cluster 20,000 genes

Real scenario The standard first look at an RNA-seq matrix isn’t every gene, it’s the most variable ones, the genes carrying the signal. Select the top 20 by row variance and cluster just those.

import seaborn as sns
from genomics_course.data import load_expression

expr = load_expression()
z = expr.sub(expr.mean(1), axis=0).div(expr.std(1), axis=0)

# 1. top = z.var(axis=1).sort_values(ascending=False).head(20).index   # 20 most variable genes
# 2. sns.clustermap(z.loc[top], cmap="RdBu_r", center=0, yticklabels=True)
# 3. do the same two modules still separate the conditions with only 20 genes?

Waffle & Waterfall

Cohort summaries · Day 01

Waffle Charts

Cohort summaries · theory

Part-to-whole as a grid of squares

A waffle is a 10×10-ish grid where each square is one unit and each colour block is a category, more honest than a pie because you can count the squares. Use it for whole-number compositions: variant classifications, cohort cell types, genotype counts.

It works best with a handful of categories that sum to a round total. Here: the outcome of a clinical variant panel, where the punchline is how much grey (VUS) there is.

Waffle · The Data

Cohort summaries

Variant interpretations from a panel screen

load_variant_classes() is a tiny table: each ACMG category and how many variants fell into it. They sum to 150, a clean number to tile.

from genomics_course.data import load_variant_classes

vc = load_variant_classes()   # classification, n
vc
classification n
0 Pathogenic 12
1 Likely pathogenic 18
2 VUS 55
3 Likely benign 24
4 Benign 41

Waffle · Step 1 — Tile the Counts

Cohort summaries · build

1 · Counts to squares

PyWaffle plugs into matplotlib via FigureClass=Waffle. Give it rows and a values dict of category → count; it lays one square per unit, block by block.

# pip install pywaffle
from pywaffle import Waffle
from genomics_course.data import load_variant_classes

vc = load_variant_classes()                              # classification, n
pal = [RED, AMBER, GREY, BLUE, GREEN]                    # colour per ACMG class
fig = plt.figure(FigureClass=Waffle, rows=10,            # 10 rows → 15 cols for 150 squares
                 values=dict(zip(vc.classification, vc.n)),  # category → count
                 colors=pal, figsize=(6.6, 3.6),
                 block_aspect_ratio=1)                   # square blocks
plt.show()

Waffle · Step 2 — Legend & Finding

Cohort summaries · build

2 · Name the categories and the message

Add a legend outside the grid and a title that states the takeaway. The grey expanse needs no explanation: most variants are of uncertain significance.

from pywaffle import Waffle
from genomics_course.data import load_variant_classes

vc = load_variant_classes()                              # classification, n
pal = [RED, AMBER, GREY, BLUE, GREEN]                    # colour per ACMG class
fig = plt.figure(FigureClass=Waffle, rows=10,
                 values=dict(zip(vc.classification, vc.n)),
                 colors=pal, figsize=(6.6, 3.6),
                 block_aspect_ratio=1,
                 legend={"loc": "upper left", "bbox_to_anchor": (1, 1),   # key, outside right
                         "fontsize": 8, "frameon": False},
                 title={"label": "Most variants are VUS",                 # title = the finding
                        "fontsize": 12, "fontweight": "bold"})
plt.show()

The bottom line A waffle turns counts into countable squares: values dict → tile → legend → title. Reach for it over a pie when categories are few and the total is a round number, here, the wall of grey says “VUS dominates” instantly.

Waterfall Plots

Cohort summaries · theory

A cohort ranked into a skyline

A waterfall is a bar per sample, sorted by the value, so the cohort reads as a descending skyline. It’s the staple cancer-genomics view of tumour mutation burden: who carries the most mutations, and does a subtype or marker cluster at the top.

The moves: sort descending, colour the bars by a categorical (subtype), and overlay a marker for a second variable (here MSI status) so two facts share one axis.

Waterfall · The Data

Cohort summaries

TMB across a 60-patient cohort

load_tmb_cohort() gives one row per patient: their TMB, breast-cancer subtype, and microsatellite status (msi). MSI-H tumours are biologically hypermutated, we expect them high.

from genomics_course.data import load_tmb_cohort

co = load_tmb_cohort()   # patient, tmb, subtype, msi
co.head(4)
patient tmb subtype msi
0 P000 5.4 HER2+ MSS
1 P001 3.3 Luminal B MSS
2 P002 8.8 Luminal A MSS
3 P003 16.1 Luminal B MSS

Waterfall · Step 1 — Rank into Bars

Cohort summaries · build

1 · Sort, then one bar each

Sort by TMB descending and draw a bar per patient with width=1.0 so they form a continuous skyline. The shape, a steep head and a long tail, is the whole point.

from genomics_course.data import load_tmb_cohort

co = load_tmb_cohort().sort_values("tmb", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)  # rank desc

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
ax.bar(range(len(co)), co.tmb, color=GREY, width=1.0, linewidth=0)  # one bar per patient
ax.set_xticks([])                                                  # individual ids aren't useful
ax.set_xlabel("patients (ranked by TMB)"); ax.set_ylabel("TMB (mut/Mb)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Waterfall · Step 2 — Colour by Subtype

Cohort summaries · build

2 · Map a colour to each subtype

Build a subtype → colour dict and map it onto the sorted bars. Now you can scan whether any subtype clusters in the high-TMB head.

from genomics_course.data import load_tmb_cohort

co = load_tmb_cohort().sort_values("tmb", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
sub_pal = {"Luminal A": GREEN, "Luminal B": BLUE,        # one colour per subtype
           "HER2+": AMBER, "TNBC": RED}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
ax.bar(range(len(co)), co.tmb, width=1.0, linewidth=0,
       color=co.subtype.map(sub_pal))                    # colour each bar by its subtype
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("patients (ranked by TMB)"); ax.set_ylabel("TMB (mut/Mb)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Waterfall · Step 3 — Flag MSI-H, Title It

Cohort summaries · build

3 · A second variable, and the finding

Drop a star above each MSI-H patient’s bar, build a combined legend (subtype patches + the star), and title with the result. The stars cluster in the head, MSI-H tumours are the hypermutators.

from genomics_course.data import load_tmb_cohort
from matplotlib.patches import Patch                     # for the legend swatches

co = load_tmb_cohort().sort_values("tmb", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
sub_pal = {"Luminal A": GREEN, "Luminal B": BLUE, "HER2+": AMBER, "TNBC": RED}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
ax.bar(range(len(co)), co.tmb, width=1.0, linewidth=0, color=co.subtype.map(sub_pal))
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("patients (ranked by TMB)"); ax.set_ylabel("TMB (mut/Mb)")
msi = co.msi == "MSI-H"                                   # boolean mask of MSI-H patients
ax.scatter(co.index[msi], co.tmb[msi] + co.tmb.max() * .03,  # a star just above each MSI-H bar
           marker="*", color=INK, s=55, zorder=5)
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("MSI-H TUMOURS ARE HYPERMUTATED", color="#333333", fontweight="bold", loc="left")
handles = [Patch(color=c, label=k) for k, c in sub_pal.items()]      # subtype swatches...
handles += [plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="*", color=INK, ls="none", label="MSI-H")]  # ...plus the star
ax.legend(handles=handles, frameon=False, fontsize=8, ncol=2)
plt.show()

The bottom line A waterfall ranks a cohort into a skyline: sort descending → colour by subtype → overlay a second variable → title the finding. Here the MSI-H stars pile up in the high-TMB head, exactly the biology you’d expect.

Cohort summaries · exercise

Compose a cohort

Coding exercise load_assay_counts() lists datasets per assay type. Waffle it: one square per (scaled) dataset, a legend outside the grid, and a title naming the most common assay.

from pywaffle import Waffle
from genomics_course.data import load_assay_counts

ac = load_assay_counts()             # assay, n_datasets

Peak Visualization

ChIP / ATAC peaks · Day 01

What Is a Peak

ChIP / ATAC peaks · theory

Signal piled up at a genomic position

A peak is a region where sequencing reads pile up: a transcription factor bound there (ChIP-seq), the chromatin was open (ATAC-seq), or a histone carried a mark. The standard view is a genome browser: each assay a horizontal signal track, stacked over a shared coordinate, with genes annotated underneath.

The reading skill is combinatorial. H3K4me3 marks active promoters, H3K27ac marks active promoters and enhancers, ATAC marks any open chromatin. So a region that is open and acetylated but lacks H3K4me3 is an enhancer, not a promoter. We’ll build that exact comparison.

Peaks · The Data

ChIP / ATAC peaks

Three signal tracks + a gene table

load_peaks() is the signal, one row per genomic position, one column per mark. load_peak_genes() is the annotation track: where each gene sits and which strand it’s on.

from genomics_course.data import load_peaks, load_peak_genes

sig = load_peaks()              # position, H3K27ac, H3K4me3, ATAC
genes = load_peak_genes()       # name, start, end, strand
sig.head(3)
position H3K27ac H3K4me3 ATAC
0 0.00000 0.069866 0.048841 0.000581
1 20.02002 0.053866 0.048752 0.019810
2 40.04004 0.054921 0.019941 0.081723

Peaks · Step 1 — One Track

ChIP / ATAC peaks · build

1 · Fill the area under one signal

A signal track is just fill_between(position, signal). Drop the frame so the genomic axis reads cleanly. Three clear H3K27ac peaks appear, two promoters and one enhancer.

from genomics_course.data import load_peaks

sig = load_peaks()                                       # position, H3K27ac, H3K4me3, ATAC

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 3.0))
ax.fill_between(sig.position, sig.H3K27ac, color=GREEN, alpha=.85, lw=0)  # area under the signal
ax.set_ylabel("H3K27ac"); ax.set_xlabel("genomic position (bp)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Peaks · Step 2 — Stack the Marks

ChIP / ATAC peaks · build

2 · One subplot per mark, shared x-axis

Stack the three marks as rows with sharex=True so positions line up. Now you compare marks vertically: the middle peak is missing from the H3K4me3 row.

from genomics_course.data import load_peaks

sig = load_peaks()
marks = ["H3K27ac", "H3K4me3", "ATAC"]                   # plotting order, top to bottom
mark_pal = {"H3K27ac": GREEN, "H3K4me3": PURPLE, "ATAC": AMBER}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(marks), 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.2),  # one row per mark
                         sharex=True,                    # align genomic coordinates
                         gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.15})
for ax, m in zip(axes, marks):                           # draw each mark in its row
    ax.fill_between(sig.position, sig[m], color=mark_pal[m], alpha=.85, lw=0)
    ax.set_ylabel(m, fontsize=8); ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
axes[-1].set_xlabel("genomic position (bp)")
plt.show()

Peaks · Step 3 — The Gene Track

ChIP / ATAC peaks · build

3 · Annotate genes underneath with strand

Add a short track at the bottom and draw each gene as an arrow pointing in its strand direction (FancyArrow). Now the peaks have context: which sit over a gene’s start (its TSS).

from genomics_course.data import load_peaks, load_peak_genes
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrow                # arrow = gene body + strand

sig = load_peaks(); genes = load_peak_genes()
marks = ["H3K27ac", "H3K4me3", "ATAC"]
mark_pal = {"H3K27ac": GREEN, "H3K4me3": PURPLE, "ATAC": AMBER}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(marks) + 1, 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.6), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 3, 3, 1.1], "hspace": 0.15})
for ax, m in zip(axes, marks):
    ax.fill_between(sig.position, sig[m], color=mark_pal[m], alpha=.85, lw=0)
    ax.set_ylabel(m, fontsize=8); ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
gax = axes[-1]                                           # the gene annotation row
for _, g in genes.iterrows():
    x0 = g.start if g.strand == "+" else g.end           # arrow tail at the 5' end
    dx = (g.end - g.start) * (1 if g.strand == "+" else -1)  # points along the strand
    gax.add_patch(FancyArrow(x0, 0.5, dx, 0, width=0.18, length_includes_head=True,
                             head_width=0.4, head_length=500, color=MUTED, zorder=3))
    gax.text((g.start + g.end) / 2, 0.95, g["name"], ha="center", fontsize=7,
             fontweight="bold", color=INK)
gax.set_ylim(0, 1.4); gax.set_yticks([]); gax.set_ylabel("genes", fontsize=8)
gax.set_xlabel("genomic position (bp)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: gax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Peaks · Step 4 — Highlight the Enhancer

ChIP / ATAC peaks · build

4 · Shade the region, name the finding

Draw an axvspan across every track at the middle peak and title with the call. The shaded column is high in H3K27ac and ATAC but flat in H3K4me3: an active enhancer, not a promoter.

from genomics_course.data import load_peaks, load_peak_genes
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrow

sig = load_peaks(); genes = load_peak_genes()
marks = ["H3K27ac", "H3K4me3", "ATAC"]
mark_pal = {"H3K27ac": GREEN, "H3K4me3": PURPLE, "ATAC": AMBER}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(marks) + 1, 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.6), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [3, 3, 3, 1.1], "hspace": 0.15})
for ax, m in zip(axes, marks):
    ax.fill_between(sig.position, sig[m], color=mark_pal[m], alpha=.85, lw=0)
    ax.axvspan(8100, 8900, color=AMBER, alpha=.12, zorder=0)   # highlight the enhancer
    ax.set_ylabel(m, fontsize=8); ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    for s in ["top", "right", "bottom"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
gax = axes[-1]
gax.axvspan(8100, 8900, color=AMBER, alpha=.12, zorder=0)      # same column on the gene track
for _, g in genes.iterrows():
    x0 = g.start if g.strand == "+" else g.end
    dx = (g.end - g.start) * (1 if g.strand == "+" else -1)
    gax.add_patch(FancyArrow(x0, 0.5, dx, 0, width=0.18, length_includes_head=True,
                             head_width=0.4, head_length=500, color=MUTED, zorder=3))
    gax.text((g.start + g.end) / 2, 0.95, g["name"], ha="center", fontsize=7,
             fontweight="bold", color=INK)
gax.set_ylim(0, 1.4); gax.set_yticks([]); gax.set_ylabel("genes", fontsize=8)
gax.set_xlabel("genomic position (bp)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: gax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
fig.suptitle("ENHANCER: OPEN + ACETYLATED, NO H3K4me3",       # title = the finding
             fontweight="bold", color="#333333")
plt.show()

The bottom line A browser view is one fill_between per mark → stack with shared x → annotate genes → highlight the region. The marks read combinatorially: H3K27ac + ATAC + H3K4me3 = active promoter; H3K27ac + ATAC but no H3K4me3 = enhancer.

The Production Tool · pyGenomeTracks

ChIP / ATAC peaks · reference

Real bigWig/BED, driven by a config

From scratch is great for teaching; for real data you’d use pyGenomeTracks, a CLI that renders a browser figure from an INI config pointing at your .bw/.bed/.gtf files. Same mental model, production inputs.

# pip install pyGenomeTracks   (reads real bigWig / BED / GTF, not in-memory arrays)
config = """
[H3K27ac]
file = H3K27ac.bw
color = #379A8B
height = 3
[H3K4me3]
file = H3K4me3.bw
color = #9A607F
height = 3
[genes]
file = genes.gtf
height = 1.5
"""
open("tracks.ini", "w").write(config)

# render a region to a figure from the shell:
#   pyGenomeTracks --tracks tracks.ini --region chr1:1000000-1020000 -o region.pdf

ChIP / ATAC peaks · exercise

Classify each peak

Real scenario Use the data, not your eyes. For each peak centre (≈1800, 8500, 13800 bp), pull the signal of all three marks and decide: promoter (all three present) or enhancer (H3K27ac + ATAC, no H3K4me3)?

from genomics_course.data import load_peaks

sig = load_peaks()                   # position, H3K27ac, H3K4me3, ATAC

# 1. for each centre c in [1800, 8500, 13800]:
#    row = sig.iloc[(sig.position - c).abs().argmin()]   # nearest position
# 2. print row.H3K27ac, row.H3K4me3, row.ATAC
# 3. rule: H3K4me3 high → promoter ; H3K4me3 low but H3K27ac+ATAC high → enhancer
# 4. which of the three peaks is the enhancer?

Pathway Enrichment

From gene list to biology · Day 01

What Enrichment Asks

Pathway enrichment · theory

Is any pathway over-represented in my gene list?

You ran differential expression, you have a list of significant genes. Enrichment asks: do those genes fall into known pathways (GO terms, KEGG) more than chance? A pathway with 5 of your 50 genes when the genome would predict 1 is enriched, evidence that process is involved.

The workflow is always the same: DE → significant genes → test each pathway against a background → rank by adjusted p-value → plot the top hits. The fixing-up is multiple testing: you test thousands of pathways, so you read p_adj, not raw p.

Getting Enrichment · gget

Pathway enrichment · the tool

One call to the Enrichr database

gget enrichr takes a gene list and a library name and returns a ranked table, no account, no upload. It hits a web API, so we ran it once and saved the result into load_enrichment(); the deck plots that offline.

# pip install gget   (this call needs internet — we pre-saved its output)
import gget

drought_genes = ["RD29A", "DREB2A", "ABA1", "NCED3", "P5CS1",   # your significant genes
                 "RAB18", "COR15A", "LEA14", "RD22", "ERD10"]
res = gget.enrichr(drought_genes, database="GO_Biological_Process_2021")

# res columns include: path_name, adj_p_val, overlapping_genes
res[["path_name", "adj_p_val", "overlapping_genes"]].head()
# → we cleaned this into load_enrichment(): pathway, direction, p_adj, gene_count, gene_ratio

Pathway · The Data

Pathway enrichment

The pre-computed results table

load_enrichment() holds the enriched pathways for both directions: each pathway, its adjusted p-value, how many of your genes hit it (gene_count), the fraction of the pathway you hit (gene_ratio), and a functional category.

from genomics_course.data import load_enrichment

en = load_enrichment()   # pathway, direction, p_adj, gene_count, gene_ratio, category
en.head(4)
pathway direction p_adj gene_count gene_ratio category
0 response to water deprivation up 1.200000e-09 38 0.42 Stress
1 abscisic acid signaling up 4.500000e-08 27 0.31 Signaling
2 response to osmotic stress up 7.000000e-07 31 0.28 Stress
3 proline biosynthesis up 3.100000e-05 9 0.50 Metabolism

Pathway Bars · Step 1 — Rank by Significance

Pathway enrichment · build

1 · −log10(p), sorted into bars

p-values are tiny and uneven, so transform to −log10(p_adj): bigger = more significant. Sort and draw horizontal bars so the long labels stay readable.

from genomics_course.data import load_enrichment

en = load_enrichment()                                   # pathway, direction, p_adj, ...
en["nlp"] = -np.log10(en.p_adj)                          # significance on a readable scale
d = en.sort_values("nlp")                                # smallest at bottom

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0))
ax.barh(range(len(d)), d.nlp, color=GREY)                # one bar per pathway
ax.set_yticks(range(len(d))); ax.set_yticklabels(d.pathway, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("−log₁₀(adjusted p)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Pathway Bars · Step 2 — Colour by Direction

Pathway enrichment · build

2 · Induced vs repressed

Map a colour to each regulation direction. Now you can see whether drought-induced pathways differ in kind from the repressed ones, they do.

from genomics_course.data import load_enrichment

en = load_enrichment()
en["nlp"] = -np.log10(en.p_adj)
d = en.sort_values("nlp")
dir_pal = {"up": GREEN, "down": BLUE}                    # induced vs repressed

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0))
ax.barh(range(len(d)), d.nlp, color=d.direction.map(dir_pal), alpha=.9)  # colour each bar
ax.set_yticks(range(len(d))); ax.set_yticklabels(d.pathway, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("−log₁₀(adjusted p)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Pathway Bars · Step 3 — Threshold & Finding

Pathway enrichment · build

3 · Mark significance, name the biology

Add a dashed line at p = 0.05 (everything right of it is significant), a legend, and a title that states the result. The split is clean: stress and signalling up, photosynthesis and growth down.

from genomics_course.data import load_enrichment
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D                      # for the legend swatches

en = load_enrichment()
en["nlp"] = -np.log10(en.p_adj)
d = en.sort_values("nlp")
dir_pal = {"up": GREEN, "down": BLUE}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0))
ax.barh(range(len(d)), d.nlp, color=d.direction.map(dir_pal), alpha=.9)
ax.axvline(-np.log10(0.05), color=RED, ls="--", lw=1.1)  # significance threshold
ax.set_yticks(range(len(d))); ax.set_yticklabels(d.pathway, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("−log₁₀(adjusted p)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
handles = [Line2D([0], [0], marker="s", color="w", markerfacecolor=c, label=k, ms=8)
           for k, c in dir_pal.items()]                  # up / down key
ax.legend(handles=handles, frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
ax.set_title("DROUGHT INDUCES STRESS, REPRESSES PHOTOSYNTHESIS",
             color="#333333", fontweight="bold", fontsize=9, loc="left")
plt.show()

Pathway Bubbles · Step 1 — Add Two More Variables

Pathway enrichment · build

1 · Gene ratio on x, count as size

A bar shows one number; a bubble shows three. Put gene_ratio on the x-axis and scale each marker by gene_count, so a big bubble far right is a pathway you hit broadly and deeply.

from genomics_course.data import load_enrichment

en = load_enrichment()
en["nlp"] = -np.log10(en.p_adj)
top = en.nlargest(10, "nlp").sort_values("nlp")          # ten most significant

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0))
ax.scatter(top.gene_ratio, range(len(top)),              # x = ratio, y = pathway
           s=top.gene_count * 6, color=GREY, alpha=.8)   # bubble size = gene count
ax.set_yticks(range(len(top))); ax.set_yticklabels(top.pathway, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("gene ratio (hits / pathway size)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

Pathway Bubbles · Step 2 — Colour by Category

Pathway enrichment · build

2 · A fourth variable: function

Colour the bubbles by functional category and add a legend. Four dimensions, significance (rank), breadth (x), size (count), and function (colour), on one panel.

from genomics_course.data import load_enrichment
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

en = load_enrichment()
en["nlp"] = -np.log10(en.p_adj)
top = en.nlargest(10, "nlp").sort_values("nlp")
cat_pal = {"Stress": RED, "Signaling": AMBER, "Metabolism": PURPLE,   # colour per function
           "Photosynthesis": GREEN, "Growth": BLUE}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.2, 5.0))
ax.scatter(top.gene_ratio, range(len(top)), s=top.gene_count * 6,
           c=top.category.map(cat_pal), alpha=.8, linewidths=0)   # colour by category
ax.set_yticks(range(len(top))); ax.set_yticklabels(top.pathway, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("gene ratio (hits / pathway size)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
handles = [Line2D([0], [0], marker="o", color="w", markerfacecolor=c, label=k, ms=8)
           for k, c in cat_pal.items()]
ax.legend(handles=handles, frameon=False, fontsize=7, title="category", loc="lower right")
plt.show()

The bottom line Enrichment turns a gene list into ranked biology: gget enrichr to get the table → −log10(p) bars to rank → bubbles to add gene ratio, count, and function. Read p_adj, not raw p, and always show how many genes drove each hit.

Exercise · Read the Enrichment

Pathway enrichment · exercise

Which pathways, and how confident?

Real scenario A reviewer asks: of the drought-induced pathways, which clear significance, and which is supported by the most of your genes? Filter load_enrichment() and rank two ways.

from genomics_course.data import load_enrichment

en = load_enrichment()                          # pathway, direction, p_adj, gene_count, ...

# 1. keep only direction == "up"
# 2. significant?  en.p_adj < 0.05
# 3. most significant:    sort by p_adj ascending, take top 3
# 4. best-supported:      sort by gene_count descending, take top 3
# 5. do the two top-3 lists agree? (low p and high gene_count aren't the same thing)

Synteny & Rearrangements

Comparing whole genomes · plotsr

What plotsr Draws

plotsr · theory

Synteny and structural rearrangements across assemblies

plotsr visualises how several chromosome-level assemblies line up: long syntenic blocks (same order, same strand) plus the rearrangements between them, inversions, translocations, duplications. Each genome is a horizontal track; ribbons connect homologous regions between adjacent genomes.

It doesn’t compute the comparison itself. It consumes the structural annotation from SyRI, so the pipeline is always: align the genomes, find rearrangements with SyRI, then plot with plotsr. Reach for it when you have two or more good assemblies and want to show their differences, not tabulate them.

Step 0 — Install

plotsr · install

Bioconda is the easy path

plotsr ships on bioconda, which pulls the pinned NumPy / pandas / matplotlib it needs. A fresh environment keeps it isolated.

# one clean environment
conda create -n synteny -c bioconda plotsr
conda activate synteny

plotsr -h            # confirm it's on PATH

If you install from source instead, plotsr pins Python < 3.12 and NumPy < 2, build the env accordingly.

$ plotsr -h
usage: plotsr --sr SR --genomes GENOMES -o OUT
  --sr        SyRI output (repeat per pair)
  --genomes   genomes information file
  --tracks    feature tracks (genes, SNPs…)
  --markers   labelled markers (BED)
  --cfg       visual config
  --reg / --chr   zoom to region / chrom
  --itx       cross-genome (itx) mode

Where the Input Comes From

plotsr · upstream

Align → SyRI → plotsr

To compare genomes A → B → C, you align each adjacent pair and run SyRI on each. This is the data-generation step; plotsr only reads the result.

# 1) whole-genome alignment with minimap2 (asm5 for same-species)
minimap2 -ax asm5 --eqx A.fa B.fa | samtools sort -O BAM - > A_B.bam
samtools index A_B.bam

# 2) structural annotation with SyRI  → A_Bsyri.out
syri -c A_B.bam -r A.fa -q B.fa -F B --prefix A_B

Each *syri.out lists every syntenic block and rearrangement between one pair, exactly what plotsr stacks.

Step 1 — The Example Data

plotsr · data

Four Arabidopsis accessions, ready to plot

The repo ships a complete example: Col-0, Ler, Cvi, Eri. Grab it and you have all inputs without running an alignment.

git clone https://github.com/schneebergerlab/plotsr.git
cd plotsr/example

ls
# genomes.txt
# *.chrlen              (chrom lengths)
# col_lersyri.filtered.out
# ler_cvisyri.filtered.out
# cvi_erisyri.filtered.out

The three *syri.filtered.out files are the pairwise comparisons (Col↔︎Ler, Ler↔︎Cvi, Cvi↔︎Eri); the order of the genomes is the order they’ll stack.

Step 2 — genomes.txt

plotsr · data

One line per genome, in stacking order

Each row is a genome: a length source, a display name, and style tags. ft:cl means the file is a chromosome-length table (faster than parsing a FASTA).

$ cat genomes.txt
#file                  name   tags
TAIR10_Filtered.chrlen col-0  ft:cl;lw:1.5
ler.chrlen             ler    ft:cl;lw:1.5
cvi.chrlen             cvi    ft:cl;lw:1.5
eri.chrlen             eri    ft:cl;lw:1.5

A .chrlen is just two columns:

Chr1   30427671
Chr2   19698289
Chr3   23459830

Step 3 — The SyRI Annotation

plotsr · data

Each row is one block, tagged by type

The columns are reference coords, query coords, an ID, its parent block, and the annotation type. plotsr colours by that type.

$ head -5 col_lersyri.filtered.out

Types it draws: SYN (syntenic), INV (inversion), TRANS (translocation), DUP (duplication), NOTAL (not aligned).

Chr1  1       1084     - -  -     -        -       NOTAL1  -    NOTAL
Chr1  1085    1771083  - -  Chr1  1        1773924 SYN1    -    SYN
Chr1  1085    158550   - -  Chr1  1        157500  SYNAL1  SYN1 SYNAL
Chr1  158551  158596   - -  Chr1  157501   157556  HDR1    SYN1 HDR
Chr1  158597  270144   - -  Chr1  157557   269099  SYNAL2  SYN1 SYNAL

Step 4 — The Minimal Plot

plotsr · build

Three comparisons, one genomes file

Pass one --sr per pairwise comparison, plus --genomes, and name an output. plotsr stacks the four accessions and draws every block.

plotsr \
  --sr col_lersyri.filtered.out \
  --sr ler_cvisyri.filtered.out \
  --sr cvi_erisyri.filtered.out \
  --genomes genomes.txt \
  -o output_plot.png

Grey is syntenic; orange/green/blue mark the rearrangements.

Step 5 — Add Feature Tracks

plotsr · build

Layer gene density, SNPs, centromeres

--tracks tracks.txt adds annotation lanes above the genomes. Each line in the file is a GFF/BED/bedGraph with its own style tags (bin width, colours, label).

plotsr \
  --sr col_lersyri.filtered.out \
  --sr ler_cvisyri.filtered.out \
  --sr cvi_erisyri.filtered.out \
  --genomes genomes.txt \
  --tracks tracks.txt \
  -o output_plot.png
$ cat tracks.txt
TAIR10_GFF3_genes.gff  Genes  ft:gff;bw:10000;...
1001genomes.snps.bed   SNPs   bw:10000;lc:sienna;...
Giraut2011_cents.bed   Centromeres  bc:palegreen;...

Step 6 — Markers, Config, Sizing

plotsr · build

The publication figure

--markers labels specific loci, --cfg tunes legend/colours, and -S -W -H -f set syntenic-ribbon spread, width, height, and font size.

plotsr \
  --sr col_lersyri.filtered.out \
  --sr ler_cvisyri.filtered.out \
  --sr cvi_erisyri.filtered.out \
  --genomes genomes.txt \
  --tracks tracks.txt \
  --markers markers.bed \
  --cfg base.cfg \
  -o output_plot.png -S 0.5 -W 7 -H 10 -f 8

The bottom line plotsr is a pipeline endpoint: align → SyRI → plot. Feed it one --sr per pair and a genomes.txt, then layer --tracks and --markers for the final figure. Grey is conserved order; colour is everything that moved.

Exercise · Your Turn

plotsr · exercise

Zoom and switch modes

Command-line exercise Starting from the full command, (1) zoom into the inversion-rich region of chromosome 3, then (2) redraw the whole thing in cross-genome (--itx) mode.

# 1) zoom a single region (note: --reg alone, not with --chr)
plotsr ... --cfg base.cfg --reg col-0:Chr3:6600000-10000000 -o zoom.png

# 2) itx mode — chromosomes drawn end-to-end across genomes
plotsr ... --cfg base.cfg --itx -S 0.7 -o itx.png

Which mode makes the Chr4 inversion easier to see, and why?

A Dumbbell for QC

Make it publication-ready

The job: summarise sequencing QC to your boss

You sent 12 samples for sequencing. For each, you have the raw mapping rate and the callable rate after QC. The boss wants one chart: which samples held up, and which lost too much.

Start with the data, one row per sample, sorted so the worst callable rate sits at the bottom.

qc = load_qc()                       # 12 samples
qc = qc.sort_values("callable")      # worst at the bottom
y  = range(len(qc))                  # one row each
qc.head()
  sample   raw  callable  loss
0    S02  94.1      68.1  26.0
1    S08  94.3      72.3  22.0
2    S07  90.3      83.2   7.1
3    S11  91.8      85.1   6.7
4    S09  90.9      85.4   5.5

A Dumbbell for QC

Make it publication-ready

Draw the bars: the gap is the story

One horizontal bar per sample, from callable to raw. The bar length is the QC loss, longer means more lost.

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))

for i, r in qc.iterrows():            # one bar per row
    ax.plot([r.callable, r.raw],      # x: callable -> raw
            [i, i], color=GREY, lw=2)

A Dumbbell for QC

Make it publication-ready

Add the dumbbell ends: raw and callable

Two dots per row: where the sample started (raw) and where it landed after QC (callable).

for i, r in qc.iterrows():
    ax.plot([r.callable, r.raw],
            [i, i], color=GREY, lw=2)

ax.scatter(qc.raw, y, color=GREY)        # raw mapping
ax.scatter(qc.callable, y, color=GREEN)  # callable after QC

A Dumbbell for QC

Make it publication-ready

Style it: percent axis, quiet grid, labels

Format x as a percentage, add a faint x-grid so rows are easy to read across, and label the axis.

import matplotlib.ticker as mtick

ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(
    mtick.PercentFormatter(100, decimals=0))
ax.set_xlabel("genome callable")
ax.grid(axis="x", color=LINE, alpha=0.5)

A Dumbbell for QC

Make it publication-ready

The message: one bold colour flags the problem

A sample that loses more than 15 points is a concern. Colour those bars and dots red, everything else stays quiet. The eye goes straight to S01 and S12.

qc["flag"] = qc.loss > 15            # the rule

bar = [RED if f else GREY for f in qc.flag]
dot = [RED if f else GREEN for f in qc.flag]

ax.set_title("Two samples lose too much to QC",
             fontweight="bold", loc="left")

The bottom line A dumbbell turns “before vs after” into one readable picture. Sort by the value that matters, and let one bold colour carry the verdict.
